title: Rohit Sharma Silences Retirement Talk With Defiant 138 at Lord's
excerpt: The 39-year-old opener became the first Indian to score an ODI century at Lord's, smashing 138 off 110 balls in a losing cause as England clinched the series 2-1.
body:
• Rohit Sharma scored 138 off 110 balls in the third ODI at Lord's — his 34th ODI century and first by any Indian in ODIs at the venue.
  • At 39 years and 80 days, Rohit is the oldest player to score an ODI century at Lord's and the oldest Indian centurion across all formats at the ground.
  • England won the match by 27 runs and the series 2-1, with Ben Duckett's 141 setting the highest individual score in ODIs at Lord's.
  • Rohit broke his silence on retirement speculation post-match, saying his "job is with the bat" and dismissing the noise around his future.

Rohit Sharma walked out to bat at Lord's on Sunday carrying far more than the weight of a series decider. After scores of 11 and 26 in the first two ODIs and days of relentless speculation that selectors wanted to push him toward the exit, the 39-year-old opener delivered an answer that no headline could argue with — 138 off 110 balls, the finest innings of his twilight years.

It was not enough to win. England, powered by Ben Duckett's record-breaking 141 and Jos Buttler's brutal 41 off 13 balls, had posted 387 for 3 — their highest ODI total at Lord's and the ground's highest in any List A match. India fell 27 runs short at 360 for 7, handing England a 2-1 series victory, their first bilateral ODI series win against the world's top-ranked side since 2018.

A Century That Rewrote the Record Books

Rohit became the first Indian man to score an ODI hundred at Lord's, surpassing Sourav Ganguly's 90 against England in 2004 as the previous best by an Indian at the ground. He now holds the record for most ODI centuries by a visiting player in any single country — eight in England — surpassing the seven scored by Sachin Tendulkar in the UAE, Saeed Anwar in the UAE, and AB de Villiers in India.

At 39 years and 80 days, he also became the oldest player to score an ODI century at Lord's, and the oldest Indian centurion in any format at the venue. Only Joe Root, with 10, has more ODI hundreds in England.

"My job is with the bat — come and play, represent my country, represent the team. The noise has been there since I made my debut. If there's no noise, there's no fun."

— Rohit Sharma, post-match interview

How the Innings Unfolded

Chasing 388, India needed their senior players to fire. Rohit started cautiously against Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson on a surface offering inconsistent bounce. In the sixth over, he charged Atkinson, edging over the slips, before finding his range against Josh Tongue — pulling him for a four and a six to race to 23 off 17 balls.

India reached 49 without loss in the powerplay, and Rohit shifted through gears. He brought up his fifty off 50 balls, becoming the first overseas batter to reach 1,500 ODI runs in England. The landmark century came off just 84 deliveries — a sweeping boundary off Adil Rashid that brought Lord's to its feet.

His 147-run opening partnership with Shubman Gill, who made 77 before falling to Rashid, gave India genuine belief. When Virat Kohli joined Rohit, the pair added 113 in 14 overs, according to Reuters, in what The Times of London called "one last dance in England." Kohli contributed 74 — his first half-century at Lord's — before Sam Curran ended the partnership.

Rohit fell in the 38th over, bowled by Jacob Bethell's slow left-arm spin, departing to a standing ovation. Curran then took three wickets in seven deliveries to effectively end the chase, finishing with figures of 4-75.

The Retirement Storm

The knock carried weight beyond the scorecard. During the second ODI in Cardiff, reports emerged that selectors wanted to move on from the 39-year-old and blood Yashasvi Jaiswal into the opening slot with the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa 15 months away. BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia publicly denied the reports, but the conversation refused to die.

Post-match, Rohit addressed the speculation directly. "The noise, since I made my debut, was there. And till the time I'm going to stay here, it's always going to be there," he told the team's social media channel. "What matters is what I do on the field. Try and contribute to the success of the team."

India's Broader Struggles

Despite Rohit's heroics, India's tour of England has been a chastening experience. The tourists lost both the T20 series to Ireland and England before falling in the ODI series, finishing with just one win from 10 white-ball matches under head coach Gautam Gambhir.

The bowling attack, missing the injured Jasprit Bumrah, was exposed. Gurnoor Brar conceded 97 runs in 10 overs — the most expensive figures by an Indian in ODIs against England — while Prince Yadav bowled seven wides in a 1-79 spell. England's 387 for 3 underscored a pattern: without Bumrah, India's pace battery lacks consistent threat.

What's Next

For Indian cricket fans in the UK, this was likely the last glimpse of Rohit and Kohli in Indian blue on English soil. Whether Rohit features in the 2027 World Cup will depend on form and fitness over the coming months. His ODI record — 11,895 runs at an average of 49 with 34 centuries across 288 matches — makes the case that class, when it appears, is not easily replaced.

India's attention now shifts to a Test series in Sri Lanka, where the rebuilding under Gambhir must begin in earnest. Rohit's century will buy him time, but the questions around India's transition are not going away.
